name: Ish-bosheth
title: Saul's son and rival king in Israel
summary: Eshbaal is identical with the biblical figure called Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel and Eshbaal in 1 Chronicles. As son of King Saul, he became the last representative of his father's dynasty. After the fall of Saul and three of his sons at the battle of Gilboa, the commander Abner took the initiative and installed Eshbaal as king over the northern tribes, with his seat in Mahanaim east of the Jordan. At the same time David ruled over Judah from Hebron, and a long power struggle arose between the two houses. In the biblical account, Eshbaal appears as a ruler without real influence, almost entirely dependent on Abner's military support. When he dared to confront Abner with accusations of an improper relationship with Saul's concubine Rizpah, the commander turned against him and began negotiations to transfer the entire kingdom to David. Stripped of his most important supporter, Eshbaal was left powerless. Shortly afterward he was murdered in his own house by two Benjaminite officers, Rechab and Baana, who brought his head to David at Hebron. However, David sharply condemned the murder and had the killers executed – consistent with his overall stance that no one should take the law into their own hands against Saul's family. With Eshbaal's death, the way was opened for David to be recognized as king over all Israel.
roles: king over the northern tribes of Israel

keyEvents.title: Appointed King over Israel
keyEvents.description: After Saul's fall in the battle at Gilboa, the commander Abner appointed Ish-bosheth as king over Israel with his seat in Mahanaim. According to the text, he was forty years old when he became king, and he reigned for two years while David was king over Judah in Hebron.

keyEvents.title: Prolonged War between the House of David and the House of Saul
keyEvents.description: A prolonged conflict arose between the supporters of David and the supporters of the house of Saul. The side of David grew steadily stronger, while the house of Saul grew steadily weaker.

keyEvents.title: The Conflict with Abner over Rizpah
keyEvents.description: Ish-bosheth accused Abner of having gone to Saul's concubine Rizpah, daughter of Aiah. This led to Abner becoming furious and threatening to transfer the entire kingdom to David.

keyEvents.title: Abner Negotiates with David
keyEvents.description: After the conflict with Ish-bosheth, Abner sent messengers to David and offered to bring all Israel over to him. Ish-bosheth's position was thus dramatically weakened.

keyEvents.title: The Murder of Ish-bosheth
keyEvents.description: Two of Ish-bosheth's officers, Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, entered his house and killed him while he rested in the middle of the day. They brought his head to David in Hebron.

keyEvents.title: David's Judgment on the Murderers
keyEvents.description: David condemned the murder of Ish-bosheth and declared that wicked men had slain a righteous man in his own house. He ordered Rechab and Baanah executed, and their hands and feet were cut off and hung up by the pool in Hebron.

versions.summary: Ish-bosheth (also known as Eshbaal) was the son of King Saul and was appointed king over Israel by the commander Abner after Saul's death. He reigned for two years over the northern tribes while David ruled in Judah from Hebron. His short reign ended when he was murdered by two of his own officers.
versions.title: The Descendant of Saul
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Descendant of Saul' is imprecise and downplays his most important role. He was not merely a descendant, but an actual king over Israel. A more descriptive title would highlight his kingship.; [major] The profile is named 'Achishakar', but the summary identifies him as 'Ish-Bosheth' or 'Eshbaal'. The Hebrew name in 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:39 is 'Eshbaal' (אֶשְׁבַּעַל), while '2 Samuel' uses 'Ish-Bosheth' (אִישׁ בֹּשֶׁת). The name 'Achishakar' is not a standard form of this name in Norwegian Bible translations. There may be confusion. If the profile is indeed meant to concern Ish-Bosheth/Eshbaal, this should be clarified.; [minor] The child is listed as 'Mephibosheth-Achishakar'. According to 2 Samuel 4:4, Mephibosheth (Meribaal) was the son of Jonathan, not of Ish-Bosheth. There is no biblical reference indicating that Ish-Bosheth had a son named Mephibosheth. If this refers to another person, it should be carefully verified.; [minor] Abinadab is listed as a sibling. In 1 Samuel 31:2 and 1 Chronicles 8:33, Abinadab is mentioned as a son of Saul, but in some translations he is called 'Abinadab' and in others 'Izvi'. The list should be verified against 1 Chronicles 8:33, which lists Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab (some manuscripts: Ishvi), and Eshbaal.; [minor] The role 'king' is correct, but could be supplemented with 'king over Israel' to distinguish him from David, who was king over Judah during the same period.; [major] Footnotes are missing that explain the various name forms (Eshbaal, Ish-Bosheth) and the linguistic background for the name change, as well as historical context regarding the division between north and south.; [minor] The lifespan 'c. 1050–1000 BC' is reasonable given that he reigned two years after Saul's death (c. 1010 BC), but the birth year is speculative. It may be more precise to specify his reign period rather than his lifespan.

versions.summary: Eshbaal, also known by the names Ish-bosheth and Eshbaal, was the son of King Saul and was installed as king over the northern tribes of Israel by the commander Abner after Saul's fall in the battle at Gilboa. He reigned for two years from Mahanaim in Transjordan, while David simultaneously ruled over Judah from Hebron. Ish-bosheth appears in the biblical narrative as a weak king, heavily dependent on Abner. When Abner defected to David following a conflict over Saul's concubine Rizpah, Ish-bosheth lost his most important supporter. Shortly afterward, he was murdered by two of his own officers, Rechab and Baana, while resting in his house. David strongly condemned the murder and had the two assassins executed. With Ish-bosheth's death, the way was opened for David to become king over all Israel.
versions.title: Saul's son and king over Israel
versions.reason: [minor] The title is accurate but could have been slightly more descriptive by specifying that he was king over the northern tribes, not all of Israel in practice.; [major] In 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:39, Saul's sons are named as Jonathan, Malkishua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal. Abinadab is correctly mentioned here, but some texts use the name 'Ishi' (1 Sam 14:49) instead of Abinadab. Both likely refer to the same person. The siblings Merab and Michal are correctly included as Saul's daughters (1 Sam 14:49).; [minor] According to 2 Sam 2:10, Ish-bosheth was 40 years old when he became king and reigned for 2 years. With Saul's death usually dated to around 1010 BC, his birth year would have been about 1050 BC and his death year around 1008 BC. An adjustment to approximately 1050–1008 BC would have been somewhat more precise.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but it consistently uses 'Ish-bosheth' after the first sentence. Since the profile is titled 'Achishakar', it could have been helpful to use this name somewhat more often for consistency, or at least explain the name relationship more clearly.; [minor] The role 'king over Israel' is correct but could be clarified as 'king over the northern tribes of Israel' to distinguish from David's contemporary rule over Judah.; [minor] The events are accurate and well documented. In the event 'The Murder of Ish-bosheth', Rechab and Baana are described as 'commanders', but in the biblical text they are called 'captains of raiding bands' (שָׂרֵי גְדוּדִים) – a more precise term would have been 'leaders' or 'officers'.

versions.summary: Ish-bosheth, better known by the name forms Ish-Boseth and Eshbaal, was the son of King Saul. After his father's and brothers' fall in the battle at Gilboa, he was installed as king over the northern tribes of Israel by the commander Abner. From his residence in Mahanaim east of the Jordan, he reigned for two years, while David sat as king over Judah from Hebron. The biblical account portrays him as a ruler with limited real power, almost a puppet in the hands of the mighty Abner. When Ish-bosheth confronted Abner with accusations of an affair with Saul's concubine Rizpah, the commander responded by initiating negotiations with David to transfer the entire kingdom to him. Without Abner's protection, Ish-bosheth stood defenseless, and shortly afterward he was killed by two of his own officers, Recab and Baanah from Beeroth, while he rested in his own house. When the murderers brought his head to David in Hebron, they were met with condemnation instead of reward. David had them executed, thereby expressing his principled stance that it is not for humans to take the life of God's anointed or their descendants. Ish-bosheth's death marked the end of Saul's dynasty and paved the way for David's kingdom over a united Israel.
versions.title: Saul's son and rival king in Israel
versions.reason: [minor] The title is precise and descriptive. It works well, but could optionally include a reference to the name forms Ish-Bosheth/Eshbaal for immediate recognition. However, this is a very minor point.; [minor] The summary is well written, theologically balanced, and informative. It covers the main aspects of Achishakar's story. One small adjustment: the phrasing "God's anointed or his descendants" is slightly imprecise – Ish-Bosheth was not himself anointed, but was the son of the anointed king. This should be nuanced somewhat.; [major] According to 1 Chron 8:33 and 9:39, Abinadab is one of Saul's sons, but in 1 Sam 14:49 the sons Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malkishua are mentioned. 'Abinadab' is named in 1 Sam 31:2 as one of the fallen sons. The problem is that some traditions identify Ishvi with Ish-Bosheth/Eshbaal. The list of siblings should be consistent with the biblical text. Moreover, Ishvi may be missing if he is not identical to Achishakar.; [minor] In the event "Abner negotiates with David," verses 12–14 and 17–19 are included, but verses 15–16 (which concern Michal being brought back to David) are skipped. This is acceptable since it is most relevant to David/Michal, but could be mentioned for completeness.; [minor] The role "son of Saul" could be added as an explicit role, since his identity as heir to Saul's dynasty is central.; [minor] The footnotes are thorough and cover linguistic, historical, theological, and archaeological aspects well. The footnote about the Khirbet Qeiyafa inscription is a nice addition. The collection is very good.

footnotes.text: The name 'Ish-bosheth' (אִישׁ בֹּשֶׁת, 'man of shame') in 2 Samuel is likely a deliberate theological alteration of the original name 'Eshbaal' (אֶשְׁבַּעַל, 'Baal's man' or 'man of fire'), as preserved in 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:39. The practice of replacing 'Baal' with 'bosheth' (shame) reflects an editorial strategy to remove references to Canaanite deities from Israelite personal names.

The name 'Achishakar' is a rarer form. The most common forms in the Hebrew biblical text are 'Eshbaal' (1 Chron 8:33; 9:39) and 'Ish-bosheth' (2 Sam 2–4). There are various hypotheses about the origin of this name form and whether it represents a third textual tradition.

The period after Saul's death was marked by a real division between north and south. Ish-bosheth ruled from Mahanaim in Transjordan, a secure stronghold east of the Jordan, while David ruled from Hebron in the south. This political divide can be seen as a precursor to the later, permanent split of the kingdom after Solomon's death.

Abner's installation of Ish-bosheth as king illustrates the role of military power in royal elections in early Israel. Ish-bosheth appears as a puppet king, dependent on his commander. The narrative highlights the tension between divine election—represented by David's anointing—and human political maneuvering.

The murder of Ish-bosheth in his own home by Rechab and Baanah, who were Benjamites and thus his own tribesmen, illustrates the internal collapse of Saul's dynasty. David's harsh judgment against the murderers follows a consistent pattern: he refused to accept violence against the anointed one's kin, just as he reacted to news of Saul's and Abner's deaths.

Archaeological finds from the early Iron Age in the area around Mahanaim (possibly identified with Tell ed-Dahab esh-Sherqiyye) show signs of settlement, but there are no direct inscriptions linked to Ish-bosheth's reign. The name 'Eshbaal' has appeared on an inscription from Khirbet Qeiyafa dated to around 1000 BCE, although this likely refers to another person.

According to 2 Sam 2:10, Ish-bosheth was 40 years old when he became king. This age has been debated among scholars, as it would make him Saul's eldest or nearly eldest son—raising questions about why he is not mentioned among those who fell in the battle at Gilboa. Some scholars have suggested that the number 40 may be symbolic or that the text has become corrupted.

In rabbinic tradition, Ish-bosheth's fate is linked to broader discussions on legitimate kingship and divine election. His short and weak reign is seen as evidence that Saul's dynasty had lost God's favor and that the kingdom rightfully belonged to David.
